“as a tune ”about a castle, in Drummond“”

Funny, but not true. The castle is named after the laird who built it, Sir John Drummond, a descendant of Sir Malcolm Drummond who fought alongside Bruce at Bannockburn. Sir Malcolm was granted land at Strathearn, where the castle stands. The nearest village is Muthill (pron. mew thill), and it’s close to Crieff.

A nice part of the world. Many a gig I’ve played in those parts - good cycling country too if you like hills.

Re: Drummond Castle

That’s an alternate title, Joddy, not the author. It first appears in the Drummond Castle manuscript of about 1730-something. It’s clearly not unrelated to the Cutting Bracken family of tunes, genetically or at least harmonically.

Glen has done a workmanlike job of setting the tune without a third, but I think that second part really needs it, to my ear.

↳ Posted by Calum on October 9th, 2021.

Re: Drummond Castle

Several pipe bands and The Tannahill Weavers (1976) have recorded this jig under the name “The laundry at Drummond Castle”. Does any one know where this-a-name comes from?

↳ Posted by birlibirdie on November 19th, 2021.

Re: Drummond Castle

I know of another tune titled “Drummond Castle Laundry”, but it’s a reel, and I’m afraid I don’t know much about it. I was on one of a thouand photocopied sheets in my collection, probably from a strathspey and reel society.

I’ve just done some research and discovered it was originally a pipe polka possibly composed by Robert Meldrum. “The laundry concerned is very pleasantly situated beside a burn in a wooded glade below [Drummond] castle, and must often have rung with mirth and glee. Meldrum, who was fond of the polka as a form, was for some years piper to the Earl of Ancaster at Drummond Castle, near Crieff in Perthshire. The earliest publication of the tune, so far as I am aware, is in Logan’s collection where it is attributed to a “Ronald Meldrum” but this is probably a clerical slip. I first heard it under the title “Faded Flowers” but that title does not seem to be recorded in any of the earlier published sources.” - Broadside to Broadband by Wm Donaldson, 2006.

↳ Posted by Nigel Gatherer on November 19th, 2021.

Re: Drummond Castle

Thanks for that clarification Nigel.
I like outdoor laundries. Where I grew up they have often been preserved even though no one has used them in a century -perhaps half a century at the latest. They are a nice place to observe small aquatic wildlife -dancing over or under the surface- and hear the warble of birds and stream. A musical space indeed! (It also inspired James Joyce who had an ear for the warble of tongues but that’s another story)

So if I understand what you’re saying, the original was a polka from which a reel was derived. -Is the jig anything like the polka or the reel then?

↳ Posted by Nigel Gatherer on November 21st, 2021.

Re: Drummond Castle

The tune known as “Drummond Castle” was published under that name in the Drummond Castle Manuscript (1734), that setting being pretty much how it’s played today.

It was published a few years later (in 1748, I think) by James Oswald with the title “Matthew Briggs” - and under that title it is found in a few English books and mss. Oswald’s setting is nearly identical to the Drummond Castle MS.
